lead: Quality of Service (QoS) lets a network treat different traffic classes in different ways. It exists because video, voice and interactive games need low delay while file downloads can tolerate delay. QoS is used by ISPs, campus networks and mobile operators to keep streaming smooth, to honour service‑level agreements, and to avoid congestion on shared links.
prereq: You need: basic transport concepts from Transport services and TCP congestion control.

blocks.text: QoS divides traffic into classes. A class can be *voice*, *video*, *interactive* or *best‑effort*. Each class has a set of requirements such as maximum delay, jitter or loss. The network marks every packet with a class identifier so that routers and switches can apply the appropriate treatment.

items: Delay‑sensitive: voice, video conference, interactive gaming.

blocks.text: The identifier lives in the IP header. In IPv4 it is the 6‑bit Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) field. In IPv6 the same field is called Traffic Class. A DSCP value of 46 (binary 101110) denotes Expedited Forwarding (EF) for low‑delay traffic. A DSCP of 0 denotes the default Best‑Effort class.

blocks.where: R_i is the reserved rate (in Mbps) for class i; the sum must not exceed the link capacity.

items: Identify the traffic classes needed on the link.
Assign a DSCP value to each class.
Reserve a rate R_i for each class that requires guarantee.
Check that Σ R_i ≤ link capacity.

blocks.text: IntServ provides per‑flow guarantees using the RSVP (Resource Reservation Protocol). A sender sends an RSVP PATH message describing the flow. The receiver replies with a RESV message that carries the required bandwidth and delay. Each router along the path reserves buffer space and token‑bucket parameters for that flow.

items: Fine‑grained control – each flow gets its own reservation.
Scales poorly – routers must keep state for every flow.
Used in campus VoIP or video‑conferencing backbones.

blocks.text: The token‑bucket model is common for policing. It has two parameters: a token rate C (Mbps) and a bucket depth B (Mbits). Tokens arrive at rate C. A packet can be sent only if enough tokens exist; otherwise it is marked or dropped.
Available tokens after time t = min(B, B₀ + C·t)
blocks.where: B₀ is the initial token count (Mbits). C is token rate, B is bucket depth, t is elapsed time in seconds.

blocks.text: If the bucket starts full (B₀ = B) the token count stays at B until tokens are consumed.

DiffServ aggregates many flows into a few classes. Routers examine the DSCP value and apply a Per‑Hop Behavior (PHB). The common PHBs are Expedited Forwarding (EF) for low‑delay traffic and Assured Forwarding (AF) for traffic that should get a minimum loss rate.

items: No per‑flow state – scales to millions of users.
Traffic shaping at the edge enforces the reserved rates.
Core routers only need to schedule packets by class.
Edge router classifies packets and sets DSCP.
Edge router shapes traffic to the reserved rate using a token bucket.
Core routers give strict priority to EF traffic and use weighted‑fair queuing for AF and best‑effort classes.

blocks.text: Consider an ISP link of 10 Mbps. It offers a video service with DSCP = 46 and a guaranteed rate of 4 Mbps, and a web service with DSCP = 0 and a guaranteed rate of 1 Mbps. The remaining 5 Mbps is left for best‑effort traffic.

examples.question: An ISP provides a 10 Mbps link. It reserves 4 Mbps for a video flow (DSCP = 46) and 1 Mbps for a web flow (DSCP = 0). Compute the bandwidth available for best‑effort traffic and state whether the reservation is feasible.
steps: Add the reserved rates: 4 Mbps + 1 Mbps = 5 Mbps.
Subtract from the total link capacity: 10 Mbps – 5 Mbps = 5 Mbps.
Since 5 Mbps ≤ 10 Mbps, the reservation fits within the link.
examples.answer: 5 Mbps remains for best‑effort traffic; the reservation is feasible.
examples.check:
total = 10
reserved = 4 + 1
remaining = total - reserved
print(remaining)

traps: Assuming a DSCP value guarantees that the flow will always get the reserved bandwidth, even when the link is oversubscribed.
Confusing IntServ per‑flow reservation with DiffServ class‑based scheduling; the two mechanisms are not interchangeable.
Forgetting to include units; writing 5 instead of 5 Mbps leads to a wrong answer.
Treating best‑effort traffic as having zero bandwidth; it can use any leftover capacity.
Mixing up the DSCP field (6 bits) with the older ToS field; the values are not the same.

quiz.q: Explain why DiffServ scales better than IntServ in large networks.
quiz.a: DiffServ aggregates many flows into a few classes, so core routers keep state only per class, not per flow. IntServ requires a separate reservation state for each flow, which grows linearly with the number of users and overwhelms router memory.

quiz.q: A corporate link of 20 Mbps reserves 6 Mbps for VoIP (DSCP = 46) and 8 Mbps for video (DSCP = 46). How much bandwidth remains for other traffic?
quiz.a: Reserved total = 6 Mbps + 8 Mbps = 14 Mbps. Remaining = 20 Mbps – 14 Mbps = 6 Mbps.

quiz.q: If a token bucket has C = 2 Mbps and B = 4 Mbit, how many bits can be sent in the first 3 seconds if the bucket starts full?
quiz.a: Bucket starts with 4 Mbit. In 3 s, tokens added = C × t = 2 Mbps × 3 s = 6 Mbit. Maximum tokens = B = 4 Mbit, so bucket stays at 4 Mbit. Therefore up to 4 Mbit can be sent in the first 3 seconds.

quiz.q: A network engineer observes high packet loss for a video stream marked with DSCP = 46. List three possible reasons unrelated to the video source.
quiz.a: 1) The link is oversubscribed and the EF queue is full (or overflowing), causing packets to be dropped. 2) Misconfiguration: the router does not recognize DSCP = 46 as EF and treats it as best‑effort. 3) A downstream router lacks sufficient buffer for the EF class, causing overflow.

quiz.q: Name the two common Per‑Hop Behaviors (PHBs) defined in DiffServ.
Why is traffic shaping performed at the network edge in a DiffServ domain?
quiz.a: Shaping enforces the reserved rates for each class before traffic enters the core, ensuring that the core routers can schedule packets simply by class without needing per‑flow policing.

beyond: Not for the exam. In modern 5G networks, QoS is expressed through 5‑QI values that map to DSCP in the transport network. Research is extending DiffServ with machine‑learning based dynamic scheduling to adapt to bursty video traffic. Cloud providers use programmable data planes (P4) to rewrite DSCP values on the fly for multi‑tenant isolation. To explore further, search for "IEEE 802.1Qaz" (enhanced transmission selection) and "QUIC congestion control with QoS".
